title: Trump: Congress learns of whistleblower complaint about Trump & Ukraine
description_short: Trump: Congress learns of whistleblower complaint about Trump & Ukraine
description_medium: On September 9, 2019, Inspector General Michael Atkinson notified the House and Senate intelligence committees that a whistleblower had filed a complaint about President Donald Trump’s actions toward Ukraine. Atkinson told committee chairs Adam Schiff and Devin Nunes that he considered the complaint credible and that Acting Director of National Intelligence Joseph Maguire had not sent it to Congress. The notice did not yet disclose the underlying allegations to lawmakers.
description_long: The complaint was filed on August 12, 2019, and concerned Trump’s dealings with Ukraine. It alleged that he was withholding congressionally approved military aid until President Volodymyr Zelensky produced evidence of corruption involving the Biden family or Democrats’ 2016 election activity. Inspector General Michael Atkinson found the complaint credible and sent it, with his report, to Acting Director of National Intelligence Joseph Maguire on August 26. The law required Maguire to transmit it to Congress within seven days. He did not do so, reasoning that the allegations did not meet the statute’s definition of an urgent concern. Atkinson told committee leaders that this interpretation appeared inconsistent with past practice. His September 9 letter to Adam Schiff and Devin Nunes therefore alerted Congress to both the complaint and the dispute over its handling, before lawmakers had seen its specific allegations. After reviewing the letter, the chairs of three House committees announced an investigation into whether Trump and Rudy Giuliani had used U.S. foreign policy for political purposes. The entry records the formal notification and the emerging oversight response; the allegations in the complaint are reported as allegations, not as findings established by this notice.

title: Trump Admin sends misleading ‘buyout' offer to federal employees
description_short: Trump Admin sends misleading ‘buyout' offer to federal employees
description_medium: On January 28, 2025, the Trump administration offered federal employees a “deferred resignation” arrangement: resign immediately and continue receiving pay through September. The agreement said agencies could reduce duties or place employees on paid administrative leave, but did not guarantee leave. The offer excluded several groups, including military and postal workers, and prompted questions from a federal employee union about how voluntary it was.
description_long: The offer invited federal employees to resign at once while remaining on payroll through September 2025. Its fine print said an agency would likely adjust an employee’s work by moving, eliminating, consolidating, or reassigning a position, reducing duties, or placing the person on paid administrative leave. The agreement did not guarantee that an employee would stop working, despite the administration’s broad description of the arrangement. The offer excluded military members, postal workers, staff in national security or immigration enforcement, and other positions selected by agencies. A senior official told NBC News the administration expected five to ten percent of the federal workforce to accept. American Federation of Government Employees president Everett Kelley cautioned that the program should not be assumed voluntary. The email’s subject line, “A fork in the road,” echoed one Elon Musk had used when asking Twitter employees to accept demanding work conditions or leave. The timeline explains why it called the arrangement a misleading “buyout”: it offered continued salary rather than a guaranteed lump-sum payment and did not promise that recipients would be relieved of duties. The account documents the terms and the union’s objection; it does not establish how many employees ultimately resigned.

title: Trump: Jared Polis commutes sentence of election terrorist Tina Peters
description_short: Trump: Jared Polis commutes sentence of election terrorist Tina Peters
description_medium: On May 15, 2026, Colorado Gov. Jared Polis commuted former Mesa County clerk Tina Peters’s sentence from nine years to 17 months, which the timeline describes as time served. Peters remained convicted; the action was a commutation, not a pardon. The move followed an appellate ruling that her sentence was improper and came after Donald Trump had repeatedly urged Polis to free Peters.
description_long: Peters, a former Mesa County clerk and prominent election denier, was serving a nine-year sentence for tampering with election equipment. Colorado Gov. Jared Polis reduced that sentence to 17 months, or time served, on May 15, 2026. The commutation did not erase her convictions or restore her status; the source emphasizes that it was not a pardon. The action followed a state appeals court ruling that the lengthy sentence was improper and that Peters should be resentenced. President Donald Trump had repeatedly championed Peters, posting calls to free her and attacking Polis for not using his clemency power. Peters had been convicted of four felony and three misdemeanor charges after using another person’s security badge to let an associate of MyPillow founder Mike Lindell access county election equipment. Data and machine passwords later appeared online, and the county replaced its machines. The timeline presents the commutation within the dispute over Trump’s pressure on the governor and Peters’s election-related convictions. The sentence change altered the time she would serve, while leaving the conviction itself in place; it did not establish that the underlying election claims promoted by Peters or her allies were true.

title: Trump: Michael Caputo joins the Trump campaign as a senior adviser
description_short: Trump: Michael Caputo joins the Trump campaign as a senior adviser
description_medium: In November 2015, Michael Caputo joined Donald Trump’s presidential campaign as a senior adviser. The timeline places the appointment alongside Caputo’s earlier work in Republican politics, government, public relations, and campaigns in Russia and Ukraine. It also notes his work at a firm hired to improve Vladimir Putin’s image in the United States and Caputo’s later account that he had worked directly for the Kremlin.
description_long: The timeline dates Michael Caputo’s arrival as a senior adviser to the Trump campaign to November 2015. Before that appointment, it says, Caputo had worked for the Reagan administration, George H. W. Bush’s campaign, and the U.S. Agency for International Development. It also recounts his work at a Russian public-relations firm and at another firm that hired him to improve Vladimir Putin’s image in the United States. The account links him to a political campaign in Ukraine that it describes as encouraged by Putin. In 2012, Caputo appeared to acknowledge that he had worked directly for the Kremlin. These details describe the professional background that the timeline considered relevant to his campaign role; they do not, by themselves, establish what responsibilities he held as adviser or what effect he had on campaign decisions. The entry’s core event is the personnel appointment, with Caputo’s earlier Russia-related work providing context for why the campaign connection drew attention. It records a campaign staffing change and the reported career history around it, without treating those past jobs as proof of a specific act by the Trump campaign.

title: Trump: Roger Stone uses Proud Boys as security in Washington, D.C.
description_short: Trump: Roger Stone uses Proud Boys as security in Washington, D.C.
description_medium: Ahead of a December 2020 Stop the Steal demonstration in Washington, Roger Stone appeared with Proud Boys leaders Enrique Tarrio and Ethan Nordean, one of whom was identified as Stone’s security. Stone urged the crowd to keep fighting for an “honest count” of the 2020 election. The timeline also notes later fundraising for security and contemporaneous allegations about plans for January 6.
description_long: Roger Stone appeared with Proud Boys leaders Enrique Tarrio and Ethan Nordean at a Washington demonstration before the next day’s Stop the Steal event in December 2020. A member of the group identified the Proud Boys as Stone’s security. In brief remarks beside Nordean, Stone called on the crowd to keep fighting for what he described as an honest count of the 2020 election. The source says Stone began fundraising for Capitol security about two weeks later. It also reports that prosecutors alleged Tarrio and Nordean were planning an invasion of the Capitol around this period; that is an attributed allegation, not a finding about Stone. At the time the source was written, Stone had not been included in those allegations. Tarrio was arrested after arriving in Washington two days before the January 6 attack, while Nordean entered the Capitol during it. The timeline also notes Stone’s earlier admission in court that he had worked with the Proud Boys. The entry records a public association between Stone and group leaders in the weeks before January 6, while keeping the source’s distinction between the appearance, the later fundraising, and prosecutors’ separate allegations.

title: Trump pardons reality TV show criminals after Fox News interview
description_short: Trump pardons reality TV show criminals after Fox News interview
description_medium: On May 28, 2025, President Donald Trump pardoned Todd and Julie Chrisley, who were serving prison sentences for bank fraud and tax-related offenses. The couple had been convicted after prosecutors described a $36 million bank-fraud scheme and concealment of television income. The pardon followed a Fox News interview with their daughter, Savannah Chrisley, in which she argued without evidence that the prosecution was political.
description_long: Todd and Julie Chrisley had been convicted of defrauding banks and concealing income from their reality television business. Prosecutors said the couple obtained $36 million through false documents, spent the proceeds on items including cars, clothing, property, and travel, and used new loans to pay older ones. They were also accused of using a company to hide television income and avoid a $500,000 tax bill. After a three-week trial, Todd received a 12-year sentence and Julie a seven-year sentence; accountant Peter Tarantino received three years. On May 28, 2025, Trump pardoned both Chrisleys. The timeline places the decision after a Fox News interview in which their daughter, Savannah, said they were prosecuted for their politics, but supplied no evidence for that claim. Savannah had spoken at the 2024 Republican National Convention, and Trump later told the children about the pardons in a video posted by White House aide Margo Martin. The account also notes Trump had pardoned Paul Walczak the previous day. It establishes the pardon and surrounding public sequence; it does not establish that the interview caused Trump’s decision or that the prosecution was politically motivated.

title: Trump: Roy Cohn to Reagan: Don't forget your deal with Rupert Murdoch
description_short: Trump: Roy Cohn to Reagan: Don't forget your deal with Rupert Murdoch
description_medium: A January 1983 letter from Roy Cohn to Reagan administration officials argued that Rupert Murdoch’s publications supported President Ronald Reagan and deserved reciprocal consideration. Cohn recalled introducing Murdoch to Reagan when Reagan was governor and listed several outlets in Murdoch’s media portfolio. The letter also complained about the administration’s handling of a Boston matter and implied that Murdoch could turn critical if ignored.
description_long: Roy Cohn’s January 27, 1983 letter was sent to Reagan aides Edwin Meese, James Baker, and Michael Deaver, rather than being addressed directly to the president. Cohn said he and Thomas Bolan had introduced Rupert Murdoch to Ronald Reagan when Reagan was governor, hoping Murdoch’s publications would provide pro-Reagan coverage. He listed the New York Post, New York Magazine, Village Voice, San Antonio Express, Boston Herald, and London Times among Murdoch’s outlets, and argued that Murdoch had fulfilled that political role. Cohn then complained that the administration had not adequately supported Murdoch in a dispute involving the Boston Globe. He warned that the publisher felt slighted and could criticize Reagan if he did not receive treatment comparable to that offered by British prime minister Margaret Thatcher and Australian prime minister Malcolm Fraser. Reagan assistant Michael McManus responded that he had apologized to Murdoch and understood the importance of his work. The letter makes the relationship transactional in Cohn’s own account: favorable media coverage was presented alongside an expectation of access and support. It documents Cohn’s lobbying of administration officials and his description of Murdoch’s political value, rather than a formal agreement by Reagan.

title: Trump: Jim Mattis, former Defense secretary, breaks his silence to condemn Trump
description_short: Trump: Jim Mattis, former Defense secretary, breaks his silence to condemn Trump
description_medium: On June 3, 2020, former Defense Secretary Jim Mattis publicly criticized the Trump administration’s response to protests and its use of the military in Washington. It was his first extended public statement about President Donald Trump since resigning in December 2018. Mattis argued that treating U.S. cities as a military “battlespace” threatened constitutional rights and the bond between the armed forces and civilian society.
description_long: Mattis’s statement responded to the week’s protests and the administration’s handling of public order in Washington, D.C. He said demonstrators were demanding equal justice and warned against allowing a small number of lawbreakers to define the larger protests. Drawing on his oath to defend the Constitution, Mattis said he had never expected troops to be ordered to violate fellow citizens’ rights or to take part in a photo opportunity for the commander in chief. He rejected describing American cities as a battlespace for the military to dominate. In his view, using troops domestically should be rare and at a governor’s request; militarizing the response risked creating a false conflict between the armed forces and civilian society. Mattis said that could weaken public trust in service members and that state and local civilian leaders were responsible for public order. The June 3 statement was notable because Mattis had not spoken at length about Trump since leaving the Defense Department in December 2018. It was a former cabinet secretary’s public rebuke of the administration’s approach, grounded in his stated concerns about constitutional protections, civilian authority, and the military’s role at home.

title: Trump: Federal employees ordered to report ‘DEI' coworkers to OPM for termination
description_short: Trump: Federal employees ordered to report ‘DEI' coworkers to OPM for termination
description_medium: Beginning January 21, 2025, federal employees received Trump administration emails directing them to report coworkers whose positions involved diversity, equity, inclusion, or accessibility to the Office of Personnel Management. The messages warned of consequences for failing to report and gave employees 10 days. They also asked staff to flag changes in job or contract descriptions made since November 5, 2024, to obscure a DEIA connection.
description_long: The emails instructed federal employees to tell the Office of Personnel Management about coworkers whose work related to diversity, equity, inclusion, and accessibility. They warned that employees could face consequences for failing to report and gave them 10 days to identify positions supervisors might have missed. The instructions also asked workers to report changes made since November 5, 2024, to contract or personnel descriptions that might conceal a connection to DEIA or similar ideas. The messages claimed some agencies were disguising programs through coded language. The timeline says the emails continued on the following day and situates them after an executive order Trump signed the night before. The request reached beyond agency leaders by making employees responsible for identifying colleagues and positions for review. It could also expose supervisors who had tried to shield workers from the administration’s effort to end DEIA programs, though the source presents that as a possible consequence rather than a documented result. The entry records the reporting directive and its terms; it does not identify particular employees who were reported or establish that every reported position was eliminated. Its focus is the administration’s use of OPM and workplace reporting to implement its DEIA policy across federal agencies.

title: Trump: I'm asking Reagan to make me ambassador to the Soviet Union
description_short: Trump: I'm asking Reagan to make me ambassador to the Soviet Union
description_medium: In an account published in 1986, physician Bernard Lown recalled a lunch with Donald Trump in which Trump asked about Lown’s meeting with Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev. Lown said he thought they would discuss cardiovascular research funding. Instead, Trump described asking Ronald Reagan to make him an ambassador to the Soviet Union and claimed he could end the Cold War within an hour.
description_long: The timeline places the encounter in spring 1986 but says the exact day is unknown. Nobel Peace Prize-winning physician Bernard Lown recalled that he met Trump for lunch expecting to discuss support for cardiovascular research. Trump instead questioned him about a recent meeting with Mikhail Gorbachev and what the Soviet leader was like. Lown said Trump told him he planned to call his “good friend Ronnie”—President Ronald Reagan—and ask to become a U.S. ambassador empowered to negotiate with Gorbachev. According to Lown, Trump said he would go to Moscow and end the Cold War within an hour. Lown spent about 20 minutes answering questions and said it was the only time he met Trump. The account is a retrospective anecdote attributed to Lown and cited to a 1984 New York Times source in the timeline; it does not show that Trump was appointed, had an official diplomatic channel, or met Gorbachev. Its significance here is the contrast between the research meeting Lown expected and Trump’s reported interest in a high-profile role in U.S.–Soviet relations. The source presents the conversation as evidence of Trump’s ambition and public interest in Russia, not as an implemented foreign-policy plan.
